extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Euclidean geometry (teachers, historians of mathematics, classical geometry students)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and presents the geometric propositions and constructions (Book IV of Euclid) for inscribing and circumscribing circles and regular polygons, with associated proofs and editorial commentary. Focuses on compass-and-straightedge constructions and the cases/remarks that accompany them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5: About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABC be the given triangle; thus it is required to circumscribe a circle about the given triangle ABC. Construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (drawn at D and E) and let DF, EF be drawn at right angles to AD, AC meeting at F; then join FA, FB, FC. If F lies within/on/outside the triangle, show AF = BF = CF so the circle with centre F through A,B,C is the circumcircle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect AB and AC at D and E, draw DF and EF perpendicular to the bisectors to meet at F, join FA, FB, FC. Handle three cases separately (F inside triangle, on BC, outside triangle) — in each case AD = DB and DF common and right angles give AF = FB, etc., hence F is circumcentre. Remarks: Euclid omits an explicit proof that the perpendicular bisectors meet; Simson and Todhunter supply additional arguments about why DF and EF must meet (rejecting parallel case) and discuss case distinctions. Also notes on relation between location of centre and angle BAC: if centre inside, angle BAC < right; on BC, angle is right; outside, > right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6: In a given circle to inscribe a square
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCD be the given circle; required to inscribe a square in the circle ABCD. Draw two diameters AC and BD at right angles; join AB, BC, CD, DA to form a quadrilateral which is equilateral and right-angled, hence a square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take two perpendicular diameters and join consecutive endpoints. Proof: show corresponding sides equal because radii and right-angle relations give equal bases; show angles are right because subtended by semicircles. Conclude the quadrilateral is equilateral and right-angled, thus a square. Commentary: this and following problems consider regular figures and discuss indeterminacy for general quadrilaterals (infinite solutions) except when additional conditions (e.g., being a square) make construction determinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7: About a given circle to circumscribe a square
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCD be the given circle; required to circumscribe a square about the circle ABCD. Draw two perpendicular diameters AC and BD; through A, B, C, D draw tangents FG, GH, HK, KF touching the circle; the quadrilateral of tangents FGHK is equilateral and right-angled, hence a square circumscribing the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw perpendicular diameters, then tangents at the endpoints. Use: radius to point of contact is perpendicular to tangent; deduce parallelogram relations and equalities of tangent segment lengths to show FGHK equilateral; show right angles at vertices via parallelogram properties to conclude it's a square. Remarks: method generalizes to inscribing/circumscribing equiangular polygons by taking successive radii and drawing tangents; includes condition when the circumscribed polygon will have the same form as the given one (requires an inscribed circle in the polygon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8: In a given square to inscribe a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCD be the given square; required to inscribe a circle in the given square. Bisect AD and AB at F (and corresponding point) and through F draw lines parallel to sides to form four equal perpendicular distances from an interior point G; the circle with centre G and radius equal to those distances is inscribed and touches all four sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect two adjacent sides, draw lines through the midpoint parallel to sides to locate the centre G equidistant from all sides. Proof: show equality of those perpendicular segments (parallelogram/opposite sides equal) so circle with centre G meets all four equal distances; show it touches sides because perpendicular from centre to a tangent is right angle; reject cutting case by contradiction. Remarks: general observation that a circle can be inscribed in any quadrilateral whose sums of opposite sides are equal (special cases: square, rhombus, kite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9: About a given square to circumscribe a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCD be the given square; required to circumscribe a circle about the square. Join the diagonals AC and BD meeting at E (the centre); show EA = EB = EC = ED so the circle with centre E and radius EA passes through A,B,C,D and circumscribes the square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: join diagonals; their intersection is the common centre equidistant from vertices. Proof: use equal sides and common diagonals to show triangle congruences and equal radii. Conclude the circle with centre E passes through all vertices. Remarks: Q.E.F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10: To construct an isosceles triangle having each base angle double the remaining one
rubrics_metrics.description: Given straight line AB, cut it at C so that the rectangle contained by AB and BC equals the square on CA; with centre A and radius AB describe a circle and fit chord BD equal to AC; join AD and DC and circumscribe circle around triangle ACD; BD will touch that circle and various angle equalities lead to an isosceles triangle ABD in which each base angle is double the vertex angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction reduces to dividing AB at C so that AB·BC = (AC)^2 (application producing the golden-section style relation). Steps: take chord BD equal to AC not greater than diameter; show BD tangent to circumcircle of ACD, derive angle equalities via alternate segment theorem to get base angles double apex angle. Remarks: connects to Pythagorean/Pythagorean-descended constructions and the golden section; commentary about Pythagorean origins and historical notes from Proclus/Todhunter/De Morgan. Also shows this triangle gives a method to divide a right angle into five equal parts (useful for pentagon construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11: In a given circle to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be the given circle; set out an isosceles triangle FGH whose base angles are each double the vertex angle, then inscribe in the circle a triangle ACD equiangular to FGH so angle CAD equals angle at F; bisect appropriate angles to obtain five equal arcs and thus five equal chords AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, yielding an equilateral and equiangular pentagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: use the special isosceles triangle from Prop. 10 as an angle template, inscribe a corresponding triangle in the circle, bisect angles to get five equal central/circumferential arcs and hence equal chords. Proof: equal arcs → equal chords → equilateral; add equalities of arc sums to deduce equiangularity. Remarks: De Morgan notes an alternative more direct method; the construction is historically related to the pentagram; additional methods using tangents and centre produce circumscribed pentagon variants (see Prop. 12 and commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12: About a given circle to circumscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABCDE, construct tangents at five suitably chosen points (using the isosceles triangle construction and angle divisions); join the tangent points to form a pentagon GHKLM circumscribed about the circle which is equilateral and equiangular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: from centre take successive radii making angles equal to supplements of the polygon's angles, draw tangents at their extremities; using right-angle relations between radius and tangent and Pythagorean equalities one proves equality of tangent segments leading to an equilateral, equiangular circumscribed pentagon. Remarks: this and related propositions (iv.12–14) serve to construct/circumscribe regular polygons of various numbers of sides and provide porisms about inscribing and circumscribing polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 13: In a given pentagon equilateral and equiangular to inscribe a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be an equilateral and equiangular pentagon; bisect two adjacent interior angles and let their bisectors meet at F; join F to vertices and drop perpendiculars from F to sides. The equal perpendiculars from F to the sides show F is equidistant from all sides, so the circle with centre F tangent to sides is inscribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect angles (e.g., B and D), intersection F is incenter; join FB, FA, FE and drop perpendiculars to sides to measure equal tangential distances. Proof: use isosceles triangle congruences to show equal perpendiculars; circle with centre F and radius equal to these perpendiculars touches all sides. Remarks: includes rejection of cutting case via right-angle tangency reasoning; Q.E.F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 14: About a given pentagon equilateral and equiangular to circumscribe a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDE be an equilateral and equiangular pentagon; bisect adjacent angles and let bisectors meet at F; join F to vertices; prove FA = FB = FC = FD = FE so circle with centre F through vertices is circumscribed about the pentagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: angle bisectors intersect at a point equidistant from vertices; prove equality of segments via angle equalities and congruences (show FC = FD etc.), then circle with centre F through vertices passes through all vertices. Remarks: symmetric to Prop.13; Q.E.F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15: In a given circle to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ABCDEF be the given circle; draw a diameter AD, take centre G, with centre D and radius DG describe circle through E and C, join EG and CG and extend them to meet the circle at B and F respectively; join consecutive vertices to obtain hexagon ABCDEF which is equilateral and equiangular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: use diameters and equal-radius circles to produce chords equal to radii; show triangle EGD equilateral so angle EGD = one-third of two right angles; deduce equal central angles for the six arcs, hence equal circumferences and equal chords AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, FA and equal angles → hexagon equilateral and equiangular. Remarks: standard construction producing regular hexagon by marking off radii around the circle; Q.E.F.
